question.worked_solution:
If we plug in $x=0$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so  we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{{e}^{x}-x-1} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{[{x}^{2}]^{′}}{[{e}^{x}-x-1]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2x}{{e}^{x}-1}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{x}^{2}}{x-1+{e}^{x}} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2x}{{e}^{x}-1} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{[2x]^{′}}{[{e}^{x}-1]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{2}{{e}^{x}} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{0}} \\  & =\frac{2}{1} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$
